storm.summary_layperson: Clear evening with no storm threat — radar is completely clean, no cells anywhere in range, and atmospheric energy for thunderstorms is essentially zero tonight.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No storms approaching, so Long Island Sound's usual buffering effect on coastal weather has nothing to act on this evening.
storm.detail_html:
The radar picture is completely clear. KOKX (Upton, NY) shows zero storm cells in any approach sector as of its most recent scan, and storm motion data is unavailable simply because there is nothing to track. No NWS watches, warnings, or advisories are in effect for this area.

Atmospheric instability is at the floor: HRRR-derived CAPE is 0 J/kg — no available energy for thunderstorm updrafts. The National Weather Service KOKX Area Forecast Discussion notes that unsettled weather with showers and possible thunderstorms is expected late Monday into Thursday due to a slow-moving frontal system. For tonight's 5–10 PM window, conditions are entirely benign, and forecasters explicitly note no concerns for severe weather or flooding.

The Sound water temperature is 73°F against an inland air temperature of 77°F, producing a weak but present stable layer over the water. This layer can buffer incoming convection in typical scenarios, but with no storms within radar range there is nothing for it to modify tonight. The marine layer is assessed as weak (4°F air–water differential), not active enough to flag as a protective mechanism.

What would change this call: a line of convection forming upstream along the frontal boundary earlier than Monday's forecast suggests, or an unexpected pop-up cell over the heated interior with rapid destabilization. Neither is supported by today's data. The next meaningful storm window begins late Monday.

wind.regime_label: Light gradient wind — no sea breeze in play
wind.tactics_blurb: Light east-southeast gradient wind in the cove — Greenwich Point provides substantial shelter in this direction, so whatever breeze is available will be on the right side of the course (the western flank, away from the Point). Expect 4–5 knots early in the window declining to drifter conditions by 21:00.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Tonight is a light gradient wind day with no sea-breeze activity. The air–water temperature difference is just 3.6°F (air 77°F, Sound water 73°F) — well below the 5°F threshold needed to drive a thermal sea breeze. Only 12% of coastal CT stations showed any southerly flow at data fetch time, and inland stations are light and variable with no organized onshore push. The synoptic gradient of roughly 8 kt ESE (KBDR 8 kt, KHPN 8 kt) represents the sole wind driver tonight.

The HRRR model was forecasting ENE 71° for this hour, but the actual station ensemble is observing ESE 117° — a 58° divergence. On a gradient day this reflects a model-initialization lag; the observed ESE direction is the right baseline. HRRR does capture a coherent backing trend through the evening (holding ESE through 18:00, then backing toward SE by 19:00–20:00 as the nocturnal boundary layer stabilizes after sunset around 8:24 PM). Applied to the observed 115° baseline, expect a slow backing from ESE toward SE through the window.

In the cove, ESE–SE flow is the most sheltered direction because Greenwich Point (Tod's Point) sits on the eastern side of the cove mouth and blocks much of the E–ESE flow from reaching the race area cleanly. The numbers confirm it: the buoy read 10 kt over open water (stale, 90 min), while RYC logs just 5.1 kt on the 10-minute average — a shelter factor of roughly 50–60%. Gusts at RYC (11.8 kt against a 1.8 kt instantaneous reading) show puffing that is sporadic and terrain-driven, not rhythmic.

When pressure does fill in, it arrives around the western edge of Greenwich Point's shadow. The west shore — the right side of the course looking upwind toward ESE — carries slightly better and more consistent flow than the eastern flank, where the shelter effect is most pronounced. This matches the SE cove geography principle: pressure favors the west side.

Shift character is a slow persistent backing (ESE → SE over the window), not the clean oscillations of a mature sea-breeze day. Don't look to tack on headers tactically; commit to the right side early to stay in what little pressure exists. Speed declines steadily: 4–5 kt at 17:00, 3 kt near sunset, drifter territory (2 kt) by 21:00–22:00. One-design dinghies will be on the edge of raceable through about 19:30 and below useful threshold by 21:00. Keelboats and heavier classes may sustain manageable conditions through 20:00. Expect significant variability across the course area — a boat on one side of the line may have a knot more than another.
